items.title: Nasdaq futures drop as AI stocks cool after Nvidia-fueled rally
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - Nasdaq futures led declines on Tuesday as AI-linked shares lost steam after Wall Street's Nvidia-fueled rally, while investors awaited this week's inflation data, the final major clue on monetary policy ahead of the Federal Reserve's December meeting.

The pullback followed outsized gains on Monday, when Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's NVDA.O CEO in a historic reversal. Nvidia shares surged 31.5% in that session, adding nearly $1 trillion to the company's market value, but eased 5.2% in premarket trading on Tuesday.

The S&P 500 (.SPX) and the Nasdaq (.IXIC) posted their biggest one-day gains since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump paused his "Liberation Day" tariff package, triggering a sharp market rebound.

"Nvidia's stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session... the return of Huang does not mean that the challenges facing AI are over," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

Semiconductor stocks were set to give back some of the prior session's gains. Micron Technology (MU.O), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.O) and Marvell Technology (MRVL.O) fell between 3.9% and 6.4% in premarket trading.

Neocloud and data-center companies, which surged in the prior session, were also under pressure. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) was down 5.8%, IREN (IREN.O) fell over 4.6%, and Nebius lost 6.1%.

Before Monday's rebound, AI-linked stocks had struggled for weeks as investors questioned the sector's debt-fueled spending and the returns it could generate.

Concerns about potential regulatory scrutiny after the Democrats' midterm sweep, along with Huang's exit earlier this month, had added to the unease.

The losses came despite Anthropic's (ANT.O) blockbuster market debut last week, which failed to revive investor appetite for the sector. The AI lab's shares briefly went below their IPO price of $83 in premarket trading, down 4.4%, on track for a third straight day of declines.

At 7:04 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis were down 194 points, or 0.39%, and S&P 500 E-minis were down 61.5 points, or 0.85%. Nasdaq 100 E-minis were down 440 points, or 1.64%.

Adding to policymakers' recent calls for caution, New York Fed President John Williams said on Monday that persistently high inflation continued to point to tighter monetary policy. He added that the pace of any further rate increases would depend on incoming economic data.

Wednesday's US PCE inflation report will be the final major data release before the year's last Federal Open Market Committee meeting and a key test for markets.

"While Jensen Huang is undoubtedly important for financial markets, in our view dovish Fed comments are the only way to stabilize tech stocks and global indices in the long term," Brooks added.

Money markets show traders are fully pricing in a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike next month and see a slim chance of a 50-basis-point move, up from zero a day earlier, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

Among individual movers, Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE.N) fell 12% after the company reported fourth-quarter results.

Discount retailer Dollar Tree (DLTR.O) gained 8.6% after raising its annual profit forecast.

Reporting by Ragini Mathur and Avinash P in Bengaluru; Editing by Maju Samuel

items.title: Black Southerners say Democrats wrote them off. Their votes may have changed that.
items.content_html:
HATTIESBURG, Mississippi, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The sun rises every day over a memorial to civil rights leader Vernon Dahmer, murdered in 1966 by the Ku Klux Klan for paying poll taxes for fellow Black voters. Then at dusk, it sets on a 1910 Confederate monument, a symbol of racism to some, just yards away in Hattiesburg, Mississippi.

Melanie Sowell has renewed hope the dark legacy that has long hung over this Southern city will eventually lift.

“One day, if we continue this fight, the sun will set on the segregation, the racism and hatred that we live with every day and fight so hard to combat,” said Sowell, 57, chair of the Forrest County Democratic Party in Hattiesburg.

That hope came closer to reality when Scott Colom, a state district attorney, upset incumbent Republican US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month's midterm elections, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, the period after the Civil War. Colom won Forrest County, which includes Hattiesburg, by 11 percentage points, though President Donald Trump carried it by 18 points in 2024.

As in Hattiesburg, Black voters across the South helped deliver upset victories for Democrats in proportions not seen in generations.

Black political leaders and organizers have argued for years that Democrats could build lasting political power in the region if the party invested in its large Black electorate rather than writing off Republican-dominated states.

Expanded Black voter mobilization efforts offer a potential blueprint for how Democrats can strengthen their position ahead of 2028 US elections, according to interviews with more than 15 grassroots organizers, political strategists and civil rights scholars.

The question now is whether Mississippi, home to the largest share of Black residents of any state, was an anomaly or an example of a broader phenomenon: a reservoir of Black political power and a growing multiracial coalition that Democrats have underestimated.

The will is there, according to interviews with 19 Mississippi voters. Many say there is palpable energy stemming from anger and frustration that voting rights, jobs and identities are under attack.

“We have done so much to try to get power back in the hands of the people,” said Gloria McCray-Watson, 63, an academic counselor at Jackson State University in Jackson, Mississippi. “And I feel like we got sick and tired.”

UNDERINVESTMENT

For decades, many Democratic strategists have centered national plans on a narrow map of battleground states, leaving much of the South with little sustained party infrastructure or campaign investment.

Marc Morial, president of the civil rights nonprofit National Urban League, said the shift occurred after former President Bill Clinton’s 1990s campaigns, which focused on winning Black votes while also appealing to moderate and conservative white voters. Since then, the Democratic Party has made a long-term retreat from grassroots organizing, candidate recruitment and voter registration, Morial said.

Stacey Abrams, former Georgia gubernatorial candidate, and Black-led organizations spent years restarting grassroots work to turn a once reliably Republican state into a swing state. Democrats won two statewide seats in Georgia, including the governor’s race, in which Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected state governor in US history.

“Black-led organizations never stopped investing where our people are,” said Melanie Campbell, president of the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, a nonprofit that worked with the NAACP’s “All Roads Lead to the South” voter engagement campaign along with 160 other local organizations.

In Alabama, Democratic US Representative Shomari Figures won reelection despite a dramatic redrawing of his district to make it more favorable to Republicans. Trump had carried the new areas by about 14 points in 2024.

Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson, a Democrat, ran in a Memphis-area district that Republicans also reshaped. They pushed through a new congressional map that split the Memphis-based district into three. He lost by roughly 1.1 points.

“The important lesson to be learned here is that the Democratic Party’s future flows through the South,” Morial said. “Many of us have been saying over the years that the underinvestment meant that you would have low Black voter turnout in presidential and Senate elections.”

The party, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, defended its approach, saying Senate Democrats flipped nine seats in 2026, including seven in states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. The committee said it remained focused on expanding the map and would “work to flip every seat we can in 2028.”

“In the face of a difficult map and being massively outspent across the country, Senate Democrats made history by flipping 9 Senate seats, including 7 states Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024,” a DSCC spokesperson said in a statement.

Though Colom won his election, it came down to “affidavit ballots” — those set aside by poll workers from voters they cannot immediately verify and later counted by hand by officials in court. That process would have been unnecessary if the party invested earlier, widening its margin, according to a dozen party insiders and operatives in the state.

Canvassers in Forrest County such as Seija Hunter had to improvise with limited resources. The 39-year-old nursing assistant said she had only Colom’s name.

“When we started out, we didn’t even have any flyers, so we were going to people’s houses and people would ask us, ‘What does he look like?’” she said. “All we had was a sample ballot.”

REPUBLICANS CITE COST OF LIVING FRUSTRATION

High Black voter turnout is not the whole story, said Williamson County, Tennessee, Republican Party Chair Steve Hickey. Republican losses across the South were a culmination of voter frustration over the cost of living and failure of the party to sustain the economic message that helped Trump win a second term in 2024, he said.

NBC News exit polls show the cost of living weighed on Tennessee voters, with 82% calling it a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Still, 51% said Republicans were better able to handle the economy, compared with 36% for Democrats.

Some Republican strategists caution against viewing Democratic gains as permanent. Diante Johnson, president of the Black Conservative Federation, said the Republican Party’s midterm defeat was driven by lower engagement from Make America Great Again supporters, diminished turnout among young men and lack of funding for conservative grassroots organizations.

“This is the first year since 2016 we did not do any door-knocking or grassroots on the ground. Grassroots has to be funded and it wasn’t funded this go around. A campaign is not a campaign without the coalitions,” Johnson said.

The coalition behind Colom extended beyond Black voters, about 97% of whom backed him, according to NBC exit poll data. About 27% of white voters backed Colom, as did about 9% of those who said they voted for Trump in 2024.

Turnout must remain high for Democrats to hold the ground they gained, said Deborah Delgado, 74, the first Black woman elected to Hattiesburg's city council. She worries that Republicans, who hold the governorship and control both chambers of the state legislature, could enact more partisan electoral maps or tighter voting restrictions.

‘ACTIVATED’ BLACK VOTERS

Leaders say much of voters' motivation came from the Trump administration’s own actions. Federal workforce cuts caused a cascade of job losses among Black voters, said CJ Rhodes, pastor of Mt. Helm Baptist Church in Jackson, Mississippi.

Coupled with the administration’s push to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programs and the Supreme Court’s decision to weaken the Voting Rights Act, Rhodes said Black voters across the state were “activated.”

Across Mississippi and South Carolina, nonpartisan voter registration group Registration Nation identified thousands of unregistered Black voters and sought to turn them into votes. It said sustained investment will be crucial.

“You can’t let people vote and then go away,” said Andrea Pringle, president of the organization.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: JD Vance's ties to prized Venezuelan oil contract under investigation by US Senate panel
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - A US Senate committee is investigating whether US Vice President JD Vance played a role in the awarding of a lucrative Venezuelan oil deal to commodities giant Vitol, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

The investigation follows an exclusive Reuters report that detailed a meeting between Vance and Vitol trader John Addison a week before the United States invaded Venezuela in January and captured authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro.

"I write today with serious concern that you may have used your position as Vice President to help a major political donor secure lucrative business opportunities involving Venezuelan oil," according to the letter, sent to Vance by Senator Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat.

Hassan will become chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January when the new Congress is seated. She's seeking a number of documents from Vance's office by December 14. Among them are communications between Vance or his staff and Addison or the trading firm.

The meeting between Vance and Addison happened in December 2025 during a trip Vance made to Montana's Yellowstone Club, an ultra-exclusive ski and golf resort, according to a person familiar with the matter. At the time, Addison was a gasoline trader for Vitol with no expertise in trading Venezuelan crude, according to Vitol. He retired from Vitol earlier this year.

Vance and Addison talked about Venezuela, according to the person with knowledge of the meeting, who was given an account of the discussion by Addison. Vance was particularly interested to know how quickly Venezuelan crude could be sold if the US hypothetically gained control of the country's oil supplies, the person said. Addison assured Vance that Vitol was well-placed to do that job.

Both Vance and Addison have denied having the meeting.

Hassan wrote in her letter: "Despite denials from your office and Mr. Addison, flight records place his private jet and your government plane at the same Montana airport on the day of the reported meeting."

In response to questions for this story, Vance's press secretary, Luke Schroeder, said in a statement: "The alleged airport meeting never happened."

Reuters did not specify, in the original report, that the meeting happened at the airport.

Vitol and Addison were not immediately available for comment.

Addison has confirmed to Reuters that on January 5 – two days after the operation that ousted Maduro and killed up to 100 people – US Energy Secretary Chris Wright called him at his desk in Houston with an irresistible offer.

President Donald Trump's administration was planning to start selling the South American OPEC nation's crude to global buyers to finance its coming political transition. Wright wanted to know from Addison if Vitol wanted the job.

The Department of Energy confirmed Wright called Addison on January 5 to discuss Venezuela.

Within days, Vitol and its rival trading firm Trafigura landed special licenses to sell Venezuela's oil, according to the two firms. The companies have since earned hundreds of millions of dollars marketing the crude, according to estimates by independent experts.

The United States handled more than $12 billion of Venezuela's oil revenue in the first nine months of this year, according to a report made public by the State Department earlier this month.

Addison had been an early backer of Vance, contributing $300,000 in 2022 to the Protect Ohio Values Political Action Committee to help Vance's successful bid for one of Ohio's US Senate seats, Federal Election Commission records show.

Later, Addison and his wife, Shannon, contributed $7 million in 2024 to political action committees to help secure Trump's second term in the White House, according to Federal Election Commission records.

Reporting By Tim McLaughlin; Editing by Anna Driver

items.title: US malls make a holiday comeback as shoppers seek more than deals
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US mall owners and retailers are betting they can draw online shoppers with an experience they can't get from their screens: a festive day out.

Restaurants, entertainment and shared experiences are becoming increasingly important to draw shoppers to malls, surveys show, pushing brands to offer in-store deals and revamp their outlets to make the trip worthwhile.

Some 84% of Americans planning to shop over Thanksgiving weekend expect to do so in a physical store, the highest share since 2019, according to a survey by the International Council of Shopping Centers. And about 55% of US holiday shoppers plan to visit an indoor mall this season, up from roughly 50% last year, according to a separate consumer survey by real estate investment company JLL.

Brian Daniel, 55, of Grand Rapids, Michigan, said most of his shopping shifted online after the pandemic, but he has recently returned to malls, drawn partly by the experience of shopping in person.

"When I go to the mall, I'm not just in and out. I make it an evening. Shopping, dining, and a movie," Daniel said. During the holidays, he said, the music, decorations and ability to browse for gifts add to the appeal.

Refreshments are increasingly part of the shopping trip, with about 21% of respondents to JLL's survey expecting to buy a drink or food on every trip this holiday season, up from 12% last year.

"(Shoppers are) gravitating towards malls because of the depth and breadth of opportunities to shop," said Paul Chase, president of lifestyle property management at JLL. "It's important to customers or shoppers that they're going to go where they get ... the best experience."

Consumers heading for the mall expect to spend $1,357 per head during the holiday season, about 23% more than the amount budgeted by those who do not plan to visit malls, the JLL survey showed.

Shoppers expect to spend 17.3% more on dining and entertainment and 16% more on food and decorations than in the past holiday season, while planned spending on gifts is up just 3.1%, the survey showed.

THE NEW MALLRATS

Younger consumers are helping drive the shift, increasingly treating malls as a place to socialize rather than simply shop, Simon Property Group (SPG.N) CEO Eli Simon told a real estate conference in September.

Shoppers also "want to go where the best restaurants are; they want to go where the entertainment is," said Stephen Yalof, CEO of Tanger, which owns 42 shopping centers across the US and Canada, most of them outlet centers.

To lure shoppers, retailers are bolstering their in-store mall assortments while offering new experiences.

Coach (TPR.N), for example, is for the first time selling its Tabby and New York collection handbags across its outlet stores. In prior years, shoppers could only find these bags, which typically cost hundreds of dollars, in Coach's full-price retail stores.

"We're providing access to these items wherever our customer chooses to shop. That's new," said Leigh Manheim Levine, president of Coach North America. The brand realized that Gen Z shoppers "were very confused when they saw Tabby on TikTok but they didn't see it in the store," she said.

Coach has also been "fast and furiously" opening in-store cafés, Levine said. In the past two months, it has doubled the number of Coach Coffee Shops in North America to eight locations — mostly in outlet malls with limited food and beverage options.

"Customers have so many choices today, so we have to keep earning their visits by offering something they can't get online," said Nata Dvir, chief merchandising officer at department store chain Macy's (M.N). She pointed to an on-site Levi's tailoring pop-up and a custom Ralph Lauren embroidery station.

Reporting by Aishwarya Venugopal in Bengaluru and Danielle Kaye in Los Angeles; Editing by Lisa Jucca

items.title: Army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed on Wednesday
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - The US military will proceed on Wednesday with its plan to blow up a deteriorating stockpile of toxic lead explosives in rural Iowa, the Army's top civilian official said on Monday, after a federal appeals court gave clearance to the waste disposal operation.

In an announcement late Monday on X, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle called the choice to move forward a "consensus decision" among all the federal agencies involved, as well as the courts and state officials.

"Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa's current and incoming governors say the call belongs to the experts," Telle said. "We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities."

The Army sparked a public outcry last week when details surfaced of its plan to conduct two controlled detonations of 68 drums, or nearly 10,000 pounds (4,500 kilograms), of degraded lead azide, a chemical used in munitions, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental groups immediately filed suit to block the plan, raising public safety concerns over the likelihood that the explosions would release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site, about 150 miles (241.4 km) southeast of Des Moines.

The lawsuit challenged a special permit granted for the operation by the Environmental Protection Agency.

The EPA countered that a managed detonation would be far less risky than an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion of the highly volatile material, a scenario the agency said was growing more likely as the weather turns colder in Iowa.

According to the EPA, any attempt to chemically neutralize or relocate the storage drums would also risk an uncontrolled blast.

A three-judge panel of the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals last Thursday issued a temporary stay blocking the EPA's permit while the court more thoroughly reviewed the case.

But Trump administration lawyers filed a legal notice two days later asserting that the Army intended to carry out the controlled detonation with or without court approval, citing an emergency exemption to federal environmental laws.

Then, in another twist on Monday, US President Donald Trump himself weighed in on the controversy, ordering the Army to hold off on its disposal plan until the appeals court had ruled in its favor.

Trump also said Iowa's Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, should approve of such a decision or be held responsible for "any and all death or destruction" that might result from further delays.

Sand, who does not take office until January and thus lacks any authority as governor until then, responded to the Republican president's Truth Social post on Monday by saying it was up to the Trump administration to decide what to do.

"The administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks," Sand wrote.

The current governor, Republican Kim Reynolds, said on Sunday that she had activated Iowa's emergency operations center to better coordinate between state and federal agencies, including the Army, the EPA and the US Department of Agriculture.

Hours after Trump's edict on Monday pausing the Army's demolition plan, the 8th Circuit sided with the EPA and lifted the court's earlier stay, removing the final legal obstacle. But the status of the detonation plan remained unclear until Telle's announcement on Monday night.

items.title: Trump criticizes Governor Newsom for commuting California death sentences
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - In an unusual political speech at the Justice Department on Monday, US President Donald Trump criticized California Governor Gavin Newsom, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, over his decision to commute the death sentences of 548 prisoners.

"We come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so brutally betrayed by bad government and our political system," Trump said, calling Newsom a "terrible" governor.

Trump was joined by Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel at the event, which featured families of murder victims.

"Mr. President, I assure you that this Department of Justice is seeking the death penalty whenever appropriate for crimes committed in this country," Blanche said while introducing Trump, adding that the Justice Department has sought the death penalty 49 times since the start of the administration.

Newsom's office said in a post on X that every inmate whose sentence the governor commuted would die in prison. In a video released before Trump's remarks, Newsom called the president corrupt, saying he sold pardons and abused the Justice Department as his personal law firm.

The DOJ visit comes as Trump's administration faces scrutiny over legal moves against political rivals and perceived adversaries, raising questions about the independence of the nation's top law enforcement agency.

Earlier this month, Newsom announced plans to commute all 548 death sentences in California to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. Many of the commutations require approval from the California Supreme Court.

Newsom has argued that capital punishment is morally wrong and inconsistent with California's values. He also has said it fails to make communities safer.

California has not carried out an execution since 2006, although voters rejected proposals to abolish the death penalty in 2012 and 2016.

A narrow majority of Americans, 55%, support the death penalty, while 31% oppose it, an October Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

Newsom's move offers the president an opportunity to revive a familiar line of attack — Democrats are weak on crime — as the governor weighs a possible presidential bid.

Newsom's move has drawn criticism from prosecutors and some victims' families, while supporters argue that capital punishment is costly, unevenly applied and carries an unacceptable risk of executing innocent people.

Trump last addressed the DOJ in March 2025, when he used a speech focused on crime and immigration to air grievances over his own criminal prosecutions and promised to expose what he called misconduct by officials who had investigated him.

Since then, the department has pursued investigations targeting several of Trump's perceived enemies, although judges and grand juries have rejected some cases.

On Monday, Trump brought families of the victims on stage to criticize Newsom for showing mercy to their relatives' killers and praise the president for being tough on crime. Relatives — and Trump — said Newsom was playing politics with public safety.

Trump announced actions aimed at expanding the use of the death penalty. He directed the Justice Department to seek capital punishment for murderers of children and rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims.

The president directed Blanche to expedite executions. He announced $150 million in grants for law enforcement and said he would give a 17-year-old relative of a victim $5,000.

Reporting by Nandita Bose in Washington, Editing by Ross Colvin, Michael Learmonth, Matthew Lewis, Sanjeev Miglani and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: US reports three bird flu cases, one death in Washington state, WHO says
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - The World Health Organization said on Tuesday it had been notified by the United States of three confirmed human cases of bird flu in Washington state, including one death.

All three cases were adults who worked on dairy farms in Yakima County, Washington state, where the avian influenza virus was recently detected in cattle, the WHO said.

WHO said there was no evidence so far of human-to-human transmission based on information available.

The first patient developed mild symptoms, including eye irritation and a runny nose, and was not hospitalized. The second, who had underlying medical conditions, developed severe respiratory illness and died on November 1. The third developed conjunctivitis and recovered without hospitalization.

Genetic sequencing confirmed all three infections were caused by the H5N1 virus, with strains closely matching those detected in dairy cattle in Washington.

H5N1 bird flu is a subtype of influenza A virus that primarily infects wild and domestic birds, and occasionally spreads to mammals, including humans.

While the current public health risk is low, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is watching the situation carefully and working with states to monitor people with animal exposures.

The US CDC has reported 75 human H5 infections since February 2024, including the three cases in Washington.

Reporting by Akanksha Khushi and Siddhi Mahatole in Bengaluru; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Shailesh Kuber

items.title: US bill aims to clear hurdle to medication for people with opioid addiction
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - A pair of Democratic US lawmakers on Tuesday unveiled a bill aimed at improving access to buprenorphine, a medication that can effectively treat opioid addiction but is not commonly used.

The so-called BUPE for Recovery Act, authored by US Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and New York Representative Paul Tonko, is designed to remove a regulatory hurdle pharmacies face when ordering the drug, Heinrich's office told Reuters.

Drug distributors like McKesson (MCK.N) and Cardinal Health (CAH.N) are required to report suspicious orders of controlled substances to a US Drug Enforcement Administration-run database known as SORS. Flagging can result in orders being blocked.

Buprenorphine, often called bupe, is technically an opioid, and is among the drugs that must be reported, which addiction doctors have long bemoaned. "The treatment is flagged the same as the poison," Gregory Famiglio, a Pennsylvania-based addiction physician, said in an interview.

Order thresholds are not known to pharmacies, and fear of enforcement can discourage orders, experts say. A 2025 study by University of Texas researchers found that heightened monitoring led to rationing of buprenorphine and care interruptions.

Heinrich and Tonko's legislation would exempt bupe from such reporting for the duration of the US opioid public health emergency, first declared in 2017, and would require the government to study whether it needs to be re-included after.

Though the current congressional session is wrapping up, introducing the bill now "helps build awareness and momentum," a Heinrich spokesperson said.

A previous version of the bill stalled in 2024, but Democrats will control both chambers of Congress beginning January 3.

BROADER BARRIERS

Buprenorphine, shown to reduce cravings and overdose risk, has been on the market since 2002. But only 15% to 20% of Americans with addiction use medication — whether buprenorphine or other options like methadone — to treat their disease, recent US surveys have shown.

Experts attribute the low figures to stigma on the part of prescribing doctors and pharmacists, low reimbursement rates, and difficulty persuading people with addiction to get help.

Only 38.8% of US pharmacies were regularly dispensing buprenorphine as of 2023, a study by University of Southern California and UC Berkeley researchers found.

Some experts fear it will take more than legislation to get those numbers up. In the shadow of the opioid crisis, buprenorphine still carries the stigma of a substance that can be misused to get high, although academic and medical research has shown that is a rare occurrence.

"There's this fear of stocking opioids... and being implicated in overdoses," said Dima Qato, an associate professor of pharmacy at USC, and an author of the study.

Reporting by Nicholas P. Brown; Editing by Bill Berkrot

items.title: After decades, Texas Democrats have political capital. This is how they plan to spend it
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - For Democrats, winning Texas took three decades. Now they want to move fast on their campaign promises, and are daring Republicans to stand in their way.

Texas Democrats swept every statewide office in the November 3 midterm elections, their first such wins since 1994, and took the state House for the first time in more than 20 years. Republicans kept the Senate.

As Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa prepares to take office in January, her allies are warning Republicans not to block her populist economic agenda.

“They can do whatever they want,” said state Democratic Senator Roland Gutierrez, who filed a bill this month to use an emergency fund to send $1,500 to every Texas household, a key Hinojosa campaign pledge. “But they proceed at their own peril.”

Even before their new majority takes effect, Democratic lawmakers have introduced over 1,000 bills, including legislation that would repeal a private school voucher program, expand Medicaid, raise the minimum wage and end tax breaks for data centers.

The populist promises that helped carry the party to widespread victories in this bastion of American conservatism, however, are the ones most likely to stall in the Republican-controlled Senate, analysts said. And Hinojosa, who has so far appealed for bipartisanship, must also balance the demands of her party’s energized progressive wing.

Democratic lawmakers, strategists and grassroots organizers told Reuters they see their mandate from voters as real but conditional, and they plan to turn any Republican obstruction into a campaign issue in the 2028 presidential race.

The stakes reach well beyond the capital of Austin. No Republican has won the White House without Texas since Richard Nixon in 1968.

‘POLITICAL SUICIDE’

In an election defined by affordability concerns, Hinojosa campaigned on a “high-cost emergency” -- pledging to suspend the state’s 20-cent gas tax, freeze electricity rates and send $1,500 to every household from Texas’ rainy-day fund. Her campaign put the total cost near $17 billion.

“Her most visible affordability promises are among the hardest to deliver,” said Brandon Rottinghaus, a University of Houston political scientist.

Hinojosa's office did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

Tapping the emergency fund for anything but a budget shortfall requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber, according to the Texas Taxpayers and Research Association, and would require significant Republican support. Republican state Representative Brooks Landgraf said this week he doubted the plan could clear that bar.

Chuck Rocha, a Democratic strategist who advised Hinojosa, US Senator-elect James Talarico and several winning House candidates, sees it differently.

He thinks blocking the checks “would be political suicide.” Republicans “give tax breaks to … Elon Musk, but they wouldn’t give you $1,500,” Rocha added. “The ad writes itself.”

Gutierrez has been approaching Republican senators about a kind of coalition government to keep bills moving. But he said it’s too early to tell how combative the coming session will be.

“One or two Republican holdouts in the state Senate could absolutely make the difference,” said Allison Campolo, who chairs the Democratic Party in Tarrant County, a Fort Worth-area battleground. “If we don’t do a good job messaging and informing people, then that’s on us too.”

The likeliest bipartisan deal is on schools. Many Democrats want to repeal the $1 billion voucher program passed last year, which provided taxpayer dollars to some Texas families to send their children to private schools.

Republican Senator Paul Bettencourt, who led the voucher push, has said lawmakers should review the program to see “what’s working well and what’s not.”

Hinojosa has said revamping vouchers was “a negotiation”; most observers expect her to bargain the program down rather than killing it.

But not every Democrat is in a bargaining mood.

“I’m not for vouchers, and I hope to see their end this session,” Gutierrez said.

Kendall Scudder, the progressive Texas Democratic Party chairman widely credited with rebuilding the party, called public education “the hill to die on.”

“If you want to govern like a Texas Democrat, it means you need to take on whatever billionaire, whatever banker, whatever bootlicking bastard you have to to make sure the little guy gets a seat at the table,” he said.

‘DON’T GO BACK’

Hinojosa, for her part, has projected moderation.

She has appointed Republicans to her transition team, stressed that she has no interest in fighting culture wars and expressed her intention to work across the aisle on a range of issues.

“Clean government should not be a partisan issue,” Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune this week. “It should be something that we all want.”

Democratic presumptive House Speaker Senfronia Thompson has made similar overtures.

The House “functions best when the two parties work together,” she told Reuters in a statement. “Voters expect us to deliver on affordability issues, health care, and strengthening public education, and that’s what we will do.”

These appeals to centrism have generated wariness among some progressives and grassroots activists who helped power Democrats to victory.

Texans “didn’t show up and vote because they wanted someone to be Republican light,” Scudder said.

Not everything will require Republican buy-in. With the power to name thousands of new appointees to state boards and commissions, said Cal Jillson, a political scientist at Southern Methodist University, Hinojosa can reshape the state bureaucracy.

About half of Texas judges reach the bench by governor’s appointment, he added, putting an ideological shift of the judiciary within reach.

Hinojosa has also vowed to revoke several of Governor Greg Abbott’s executive orders, including ones steering state land toward the federal detention of migrants and freezing the hiring of skilled foreign workers at state agencies and universities.

When it comes to Republicans, who held unified political control for so long, “I think they’ve forgotten how many levers of power the governor has,” Jillson said.

Democratic organizers and strategists are already warning against complacency – and testing out talking points for 2028.

“It’s about a ‘don’t go back’ kind of message,” said Campolo, the organizer in Tarrant County. “Just because we won this time doesn’t mean we win every time.”

That was echoed by Rocha, who said Latino voters swung back to Democrats because of anger at Republicans, not out of loyalty.

“This is an opportunity,” he said, “it’s not a destiny.”

items.title: US envoy 'not certain' military aid to Israel will end this year as Trump promised
items.content_html:
TEL AVIV, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has cast doubt on whether Washington would end its $3.8 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of this year, as promised by President Donald Trump on the day of this month's midterm elections.

In his surprise announcement as voters headed to the polls on November 3, Trump said he had made a deal with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu several months earlier to stop providing Israel with around $4 billion in annual US funding.

Trump said Israel no longer needed US funds, and the issue had been used as a "bad talking point" by his left-wing critics. The election that day subsequently saw Democrats, including many who publicly oppose military funding for Israel, win control of both houses of Congress from Trump's Republicans.

Trump did not provide details or explain how the funding would be halted. The US has a longstanding agreement with Israel, known as a Memorandum of Understanding, to provide it with $3.8 billion a year until 2028 to fund purchases of American-made military equipment.

In a pre-recorded interview shown on Tuesday at a conference on US-Israel relations at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, Huckabee said the MoU "is supposed to continue for two more years, so I'm not certain that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year."

Huckabee, a Republican former governor of Arkansas, said funding had been allocated by Congress and he was unsure whether it could be stopped without congressional approval.

Public support for Israel has fallen in the United States, particularly among Democrats but also among Republicans, over Israel's conduct in the war in Gaza and over the unpopular war Trump launched alongside Netanyahu this year against Iran.

Huckabee said US and Israeli officials had been working on a new MoU "for months". He did not say whether those talks had continued following Trump's announcement that the military aid would end.

Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority in an October 27 election but is still serving as a caretaker, has publicly discussed phasing out US military aid, a move analysts say was intended to preempt growing criticism in the US of Israel.

The Democrats' resounding victory over the Republicans has been met with apprehension in Israel, where Netanyahu emphasised his close relationship with Trump in his own campaign.

Huckabee, an Evangelical Christian and staunch supporter of Israel, said that he hoped there would not be a "dramatic, seismic shift" in US-Israel relations, arguing that the partnership benefited the citizens of both countries.

items.title: Social media companies not liable for Buffalo mass shooting, New York's highest court rules
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Several major social media companies should not be held liable over accusations that they helped an avowed white supremacist who in 2022 killed 10 Black people at a grocery store in Buffalo, New York, the state's highest court ruled on Monday.

In a 4-3 decision, New York's Court of Appeals let stand a divided lower court ruling that found Alphabet's Google and YouTube, Meta Platforms' Instagram, Reddit and Snap's Snapchat were immune under a federal law that protects online platforms from liability over user content.

Monday's majority said victims of Payton Gendron's attack on May 14, 2022, at Tops Friendly Markets failed to show that his actions were a "natural and foreseeable consequence" of the defendants' decisions about how to design and run their platforms.

"The shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law," the majority said in an unsigned opinion.

Gendron was 18 years old at the time of the attack. Many courts have addressed the degree to which Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act should shield social media companies over conduct by young children and teenagers who use their platforms.

Matthew Bergman, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, in a statement said his clients are evaluating their legal options.

"The families affected by the tragic May 2022 Buffalo grocery store attack deserve accountability when dangerous product design choices contribute to real-world harm," Bergman said.

Google, Meta, Reddit and Snap did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

SHUTTING THE COURTHOUSE DOOR

Victims' relatives, as well as store employees and customers who saw the attack, contended that the defendants' platforms were designed to addict and radicalize users like Gendron.

Dissenting from Monday's decision, Judge Jenny Rivera said juries should decide whether the prevalence of mass shootings would put social media companies on notice that their allegedly defective products, and failure to warn about their dangers, could trigger such violence.

"No federal or state law requires that we slam the courthouse door on plaintiffs' claims," Rivera wrote.

The Court of Appeals also upheld the dismissal of claims against Amazon.com, Discord, 4chan and Twitch Interactive related to Gendron's attack. Lawyers for those companies declined to comment or were not immediately available for comment.

Gendron was sentenced in February 2023 to life in prison without parole, after pleading guilty to state charges including murder and terrorism motivated by hate.

He could face the death penalty at a related federal trial, where jury selection began on October 13.

Reporting by Jonathan Stempel in New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: Trump rewrites the lame-duck rules with flex on Nvidia CEO
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's intervention to restore Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA.O) offered an early indication of how Trump, despite losing control of Congress to Democrats, can continue to wield power in Washington and beyond during what is traditionally considered the lame-duck phase of any presidency.

Days after the Nvidia board had ruled out restoring Huang following a series of damaging revelations about his relations with an alleged Chinese spy and other women, Trump seized control of the narrative.

He forcefully made the case for Huang's return in a press conference on Friday, then dispatched key members of his administration throughout the weekend to convince the board to reverse its position in an announcement shortly before the stock market opened on Monday.

Trump celebrated his victory with a nearly hour-long interview on CNBC in which he took credit for the turnabout and called Huang a "national treasure."

"The board decided to do what we wanted to do. And one of the things the board wanted to know: Is there a national security problem?" Trump told CNBC.

"And after a lot of research ... we said, 'No, it's not a problem,'" Trump said. "We feel very strongly that he's in good shape, very good shape."

The stock market soared. Members of Congress criticized the move. Meanwhile, Trump — just weeks from his party's historic midterm election blowout that many Republicans blamed on his falling popularity — was back at the center of the world's gaze.

He soon made a social media post, based on a photo of his own triumphant fist pump following his near-assassination at a Pennsylvania political rally in 2024, but with Huang superimposed where Trump stood in the original. In Huang's hand dangled a red bra, an apparent reference to the sex scandal he had just escaped, aided by Trump's unusual knack for bending storylines to his desires.

"He's willing to do things in a very unorthodox manner," said presidential historian Thomas Alan Schwartz of Vanderbilt University. "Getting Huang back as CEO is clearly in the category of unorthodox."

NATIONAL SECURITY CONCERNS REMAIN

It was not the first time Trump had inserted himself into major corporate decisions, having pushed deals involving Intel (INTC.O) and U.S. Steel. But his intervention with Nvidia went further by putting him directly into a boardroom decision over who should lead a trillion-dollar American corporation at the center of the global artificial intelligence race.

Trump's actions may yet boomerang. Democrats, who will have the widest majorities in decades to work with, vowed to investigate once they take control of Congress in January. Huang is scheduled to make a first round of testimony at a hearing next week.

Some of Trump's fellow Republicans joined Democrats on Monday in expressing fears that Huang's return imperiled US interests because of his relationship with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.

"Allowing China to obtain America's most advanced chips creates a significant national security vulnerability," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in a statement, promising strong export control measures.

Newt Gingrich, a former speaker of the US House of Representatives who is a close Trump ally, said on X, "There is something profoundly wrong" about Huang being reinstated.

"Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy," he said.

A BROADER PATTERN

Trump's intervention in corporate America has become a hallmark of his administration, particularly with companies considered important to US economic and national security.

After a public campaign from Trump and other members of his administration to block Nippon Steel's (5401.T) bid to buy U.S. Steel in a $14.9-billion acquisition, the Japanese company agreed to give an unusual degree of power to Trump over the company's future. The administration gained the authority to name a board member, as well as the last word on idling plants, production cuts and moving jobs overseas.

Trump's team also negotiated a 10% stake in Intel last year under a deal with the struggling chipmaker that converted government grants into an equity share. Trump had called for the resignation of Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan over his ties to China before announcing a deal that made the US government the biggest shareholder in the chipmaker.

The administration also struck an agreement allowing Nvidia to sell its H20 chips to China in exchange for receiving 15% of those sales and an agreement for the Pentagon to become the largest shareholder in a small mining company, MP Materials (MP.N), to boost output of rare earth magnets.

Reporting by Doina Chiacu, Steve Holland, Susan Heavey, Katharine Jackson, Patricia Zengerle in Washington; Ananya Palyekar, Hyunsu Yim and Harishankar Manoj in Bangalore; Editing by Craig Timberg and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: White House moves to potentially replace blocked Trump judicial nominee, source says
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - The White House has initiated an FBI background check on a potential replacement for a federal judicial candidate in Texas whose nomination was blocked by Republican Senator John Cornyn during the US Senate's lame-duck session, a person familiar with the matter said.

The decision signals the White House is considering nominating Steve Fahey, Cornyn's preferred pick to be a federal judge in Dallas, in place of Justice Department official T. Elliot Gaiser as it races to appoint as many judges as possible before Democrats take control of the Senate on January 3.

In a rare show of resistance to President Donald Trump's judicial nominees, a handful of Republican senators during the lame-duck session have withheld support for at least three judicial nominees he picked in their states. The White House has already been forced to replace one of the nominees.

Cornyn, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, last week declined to support Gaiser's nomination, blocking him from appearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Trump called the move a "tremendous disservice" during a Saturday interview on Fox News.

The FBI this weekend began a background investigation of Fahey, a former federal prosecutor now in private practice whom Cornyn has recommended Trump pick in place of Gaiser, the person said.

An FBI background check is a key step that precedes someone receiving a federal judicial nomination, though it does not guarantee that someone is ultimately nominated.

The White House also has initiated an FBI background check for a second potential new judge, one backed by US Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, to fill a vacancy in his state, the person said.

Following the Reuters report, Cornyn, in a social media post on X, thanked Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel for initiating Fahey's background investigation.

"I hope the President will nominate him swiftly so we can continue moving the process forward," Cornyn said.

A White House official in a statement said that the White House expects all of Trump's judicial nominees to be confirmed by the end of the year.

Senators traditionally help choose nominees for vacancies on federal courts in their states. By Senate custom, they can effectively veto trial court nominees they oppose in their states by refusing to return a blue slip, a form used to signal support.

Trump nominated Gaiser to a seat on the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas after the election with the support of Ted Cruz, Texas' other Republican senator.

Gaiser, a former Ohio solicitor general, previously clerked for conservative US Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito and currently heads the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, a unit that has frequently signed off on the legality of Trump administration actions.

But Cornyn objected to the nomination, saying Gaiser was not even from Texas and that the White House "was trying to jam him down our throat without adequate vetting for a lifetime job."

Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: US lawmakers criticize Nvidia decision to reinstate Huang as CEO
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's (NVDA.O) decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, saying Congress should tighten restrictions on China's access to the company's advanced AI chips and scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang's return.

Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton, a Republican, on Monday called on Congress to pass the Chip Security Act, a bill that seeks to address legally exported advanced chips later being diverted to China, where their sales are restricted.

The bill would require chipmakers to track the location of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect chips have reached prohibited users.

For Nvidia, the measure could create new compliance costs and reporting obligations.

Democratic US Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is set to chair the Banking Committee starting in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "reckless," adding Nvidia's board still owes Congress answers about the company's compliance with US export controls. The Banking Committee is responsible for approving legislation on export controls.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," Warren said.

Huang will testify on December 3 before the US Senate Banking Committee in a public hearing, the panel's Republican Chair Tim Scott said Monday, as lawmakers probe allegations about Huang's ties to a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Huang's personal spokesperson declined to comment on the planned appearance.

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement on Monday that the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang "doesn't excuse" him from testifying before Congress.

Ricketts is pushing for Congress to pass the Match Act, a bill that would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. It would not directly restrict Nvidia's chip sales.

Companies based in allied countries that make semiconductor-manufacturing tools would be affected, such as the Netherlands' ASML (ASML.AS) and Tokyo Electron (8035.T) in Japan.

Supporters argue that under the legislation, China would have greater difficulty developing its own advanced AI chips that would compete with Nvidia in the long term.

The top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, Representative Jim Himes, said Huang is still expected to appear for a closed-door interview on December 1 with three House panels.

Hakeem Jeffries, the incoming speaker of the US House of Representatives, said on Monday that Congress should include "ironclad" legislation to prevent AI technology from reaching China in the annual defense bill. That bill is a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support. A Senate version of the legislation already includes several measures to crack down on China's access to advanced AI chips.

Nvidia did not immediately comment on the criticism from Congress.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said the reinstatement showed it was critical to pass legislation to toughen restrictions on US chip exports to China.

President Donald Trump on CNBC said he had pressed the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang and that he did not think the board would have done so without his action.

Republican Senator John Curtis, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said he wanted answers about why the board opted to reappoint Huang as CEO.

"Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him," he said. "I'd like to know what changed."

items.title: What to know about US Army plans to blow up a stockpile of lead azide in Iowa
items.content_html:
November 23 - The US Army plans to destroy 68 barrels, or nearly 10,000 pounds (4,536 kg), of a deteriorating lead compound used in explosives by detonating them at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

Nearby residents have protested and environmental groups filed a lawsuit, concerned about the likelihood that blowing up the lead azide will release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site.

Here is what you need to know:

WHAT IS LEAD AZIDE?

Lead azide is an explosive chemical used to detonate military munitions.

WHY IS THE ARMY PLANNING TO DETONATE IT?

The US Environmental Protection Agency said recrystallization in long-term storage made the chemical dangerously unstable, posing the risk of an uncontrolled explosion and making moving the material risky. In a court filing late on Saturday, the government said a controlled detonation was necessary "to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion."

The EPA on Saturday said there was an immediate risk that the lead azide would explode because temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 degrees Celsius) in Iowa this week.

WHEN COULD IT HAPPEN?

The US Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit temporarily halted the detonation by freezing the Army's environmental permit on Thursday after environmental groups sued. The Army said in a post on X on Sunday that the explosion would nonetheless take place on Wednesday, "to allow for optimal weather conditions." But in a Truth Social post on Monday President Donald Trump said he ordered the military to pause until it gets a ruling from the 8th Circuit allowing the detonation to go forward, making the timing uncertain.

The detonation was previously scheduled for November 20 and then postponed until Monday after public outcry.

WHAT ARE THE RISKS?

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa, said immediate risks from inhalation should be mitigated if people are able to shelter or get away from the dust plume as it passes over them. Longer-term risks come from the settling of lead dust on homes, farms and in the environment, where it will not break down further.

Lead can cause wide-ranging health problems in humans and animals, O'Shaughnessy said. Children in particular are at risk because lead can inhibit the development of the brain and its cognitive abilities, he said.

The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has recommended that residents in affected areas keep windows and doors closed for 24–48 hours after the detonation and shut off heating and cooling systems that bring in outside air, clean surfaces in potentially affected areas after the detonation and consult healthcare providers about blood testing for lead.

WHO WILL BE AFFECTED?

The impact of the blast will depend largely on the weather forecast and the direction of the wind. O'Shaughnessy said a Wednesday detonation would likely create a plume of lead dust that would travel 40 to 50 miles (64 to 80 km) southwest of the military installation.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment to alternate locations or indoors to avoid direct lead exposure for livestock, while acknowledging that in some places, this would not be feasible.

IS THIS UNUSUAL?

The EPA says that explosive hazardous waste is "often treated by open burning and open detonation," but that disposing of such waste in enclosed environments is a preferred alternative that is becoming increasingly available.

Reporting by Renee Hickman; Editing by Donna Bryson and Bill Berkrot

items.title: Measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania rise to nine
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Pennsylvania Department of Health on Monday reported another death linked to this year's measles outbreak, taking the total number of fatalities associated with the highly contagious viral disease to nine, from eight last week.

The latest death involved an unvaccinated resident of Centre County in central Pennsylvania who tested positive for measles, the department said.

Pennsylvania has recorded 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties so far this year, including 330 hospitalizations, according to the health department.

The nine deaths reported this year involved residents of Centre, Clinton, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mifflin and Montour counties. Lancaster County accounted for three deaths, while Jefferson County reported two.

Virginia on Friday reported its first measles-associated death of 2026, involving a child, while Wisconsin has reported two deaths. New York state has recorded one child death linked to the disease.

Based on publicly reported state figures, at least 13 measles-associated deaths have been recorded in the US this year.

However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed only six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, without specifying the states where the fatalities were recorded.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

The US Department of Health and Human Services said it was "saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania," adding that CDC has provided the state nearly $4 million in one-time emergency funding for response efforts in 2027.

Last week, the US lost its hard-fought measles elimination status after 26 years.

Nationwide, 5,838 confirmed measles cases were reported this year, as of November 19, according to CDC data.

"Most of the outbreaks of measles this year have been centered in counties where a lot of Amish and conservative Mennonites live," Kathryn Jacobsen, an epidemiologist at the University of Richmond, said, adding that large gatherings of unvaccinated people can allow the virus to spread rapidly.

Although the epidemic was currently centered in conservative, rural religious communities, she said this did not mean other groups were not at risk.

Reporting by Siddhi Mahatole and Kunal Das in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara, Shilpi Majumdar and Shinjini Ganguli

items.title: Virginia, Oregon sue Musk's SpaceX over Grok AI's creation of child sexual abuse images
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - Virginia and Oregon sued Elon Musk's SpaceX Super Intelligence Corp (SPCX.O) on Monday, alleging the company profited from a feature in its AI model Grok that produces child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual sexual images from photographs while failing to put safeguards in place to stop it.

Several state attorneys general had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon were the first states to sue.

The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok's safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its "spicy mode." That mode allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits.

Virginia and Oregon accused SpaceX of violating their respective consumer protection laws. They are seeking damages, penalties and court orders forcing the company to stop violating state law.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Grok is available to users of X, the social media platform that is a subsidiary of SpaceX.

In a statement posted on X on Monday that didn't directly address the lawsuits, the platform's safety team said it had taken action to block prompts that could generate this type of imagery and worked with law enforcement to pursue people who use the platform to make it.

"The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards," the company posted.

GROK SAFEGUARDS UNDER SCRUTINY

Virginia's lawsuit cites data from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, which estimated that between December 2025 and January 2026, Grok generated and posted on X millions of sexualized images, including more than 20,000 depicting children.

Investigators from the attorney general's office in Virginia found that Grok's image moderation was inconsistent, and that the bot would advise users on how to circumvent the moderation measures by avoiding words that triggered it, according to the lawsuit.

Beginning in January, Grok told users that its image generation features were only for paying subscribers, which did not stop the images' creation but allowed the company to profit from them, the lawsuit said.

States across the US have filed a growing number of lawsuits against social media and AI companies over harm they say the companies have caused to their residents.

In an interview with Reuters ahead of Monday's filings, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said state attorneys general are acting as a regulatory force in the tech industry, including on artificial intelligence, which has faced relatively little federal regulation so far.

"In the absence of federal action, AGs have stepped into the breach," Jones said.

LAWSUITS STACK UP OVER GROK

SpaceX is facing more than a dozen lawsuits brought by individuals who say nonconsensual sexual images of them as minors or adults were generated by Grok.

In the UK, lawmaker Jess Asato is suing SpaceX after Grok users generated sexualized images of her. The company has denied the claims, arguing that obviously fictitious, AI-generated content cannot breach someone's right to privacy.

In mid-January, xAI said it restricted image editing in Grok and blocked users from generating images of people in revealing clothing "where it's illegal." SpaceX acquired xAI in February and rebranded its AI division from xAI to SpaceX Super Intelligence in October.

Reuters found in February that, even after new curbs, Grok continued to generate sexualized images of people even when users explicitly warned that the subjects did not consent. The company did not address detailed questions from Reuters about Grok's generation of sexualized material.

SpaceX is suing at least two people in the US alleging they misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

Reporting by Diana Novak Jones; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Will Dunham, Diane Craft and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: US agency to vote to ease ownership limits on local TV, radio stations
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Federal Communications Commission plans to vote next month to ease ownership limits on local radio and TV stations as it vows to level the playing field for broadcasters with large tech companies.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said the commission will vote on December 17 whether to lift the limits on the number of stations local broadcasters can own in the markets they operate in, replacing the limits with individual case-by-case reviews.

items.title: US Democrats require 2028 candidates to reject dark money to make debate stage
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US Democratic presidential hopefuls will be required to denounce election spending by secret donors to qualify for debates during the primary season, the party announced on Monday, as it braces for a potentially huge field of contenders.

The Democratic National Committee, which oversees the party's presidential primary process, is planning 12 debates that will help choose its 2028 White House standard-bearer.

So many contenders are expected to enter that the party has built provisions in for some debates to be held over two nights, with a maximum of 20 candidates in total taking part.

After their rout of Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats now face a potentially bruising presidential nominating battle, with no clear frontrunner yet.

At a gathering in Denver shortly after the elections, tensions between centrist Democrats and a restive progressive wing surfaced, underscoring long-standing ideological and generational divides as the party seeks a 2028 White House nominee.

To qualify for the Democratic presidential debates, candidates must sign a pledge denouncing "dark money" — political spending to influence elections by groups that do not disclose their donors.

The new requirement is part of a DNC effort to curb the influence of outside groups that can spend unlimited amounts to support or oppose candidates without having to reveal funding sources.

The DNC said it plans to hold five presidential primary debates in 2027 and seven in 2028.

The first two are scheduled for June and July 2027, while the final debate is expected to take place in March 2028, though the party said the schedule could be adjusted if needed. The locations of the early debates will be announced in January, the DNC said.

To demonstrate that they have voter support, candidates will also have to meet polling and grassroots fundraising requirements to qualify for the debates.

Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Paul Simao
